Getting your images in

Source: vignettes/articles/getting-images-in.Rmd
getting-images-in.Rmd

tidymontage reads TIFF and OME-TIFF files. Microscopes usually save their own formats, such as CZI (Zeiss), ND2 (Nikon), LIF (Leica) or OIR (Olympus). This article shows how to convert them to OME-TIFF, the format tidymontage reads best: channel names, colours, pixel size and z-steps are kept in its metadata.

Single files: ZEN or Fiji

For a few files, export them from the microscope software or Fiji:

  • ZEN (including the free ZEN lite): use its OME-TIFF export (in recent versions an OME TIFF-Export method under Processing; menus differ between ZEN versions).
  • Fiji: open the file with Bio-Formats, then File > Save As > OME-TIFF…. Keep the options that write z-slices, time points and channels into separate files unticked, so each image becomes one file.

Whichever you use, the file name must end in .ome.tif. With only .tif, Bio-Formats writes a plain TIFF without the OME metadata, even from the OME-TIFF dialog.

Many files: bfconvert

For whole folders, use bfconvert, the command line tool of Bio-Formats (the library Fiji uses to read microscope files). It reads about 150 formats and needs Java. There are several ways to get it; pick the first one that fits your computer.

Option 1: pixi, with Java included (recommended)

pixi installs command line tools into your user folder, without admin rights, on macOS, Linux and Windows. The Bio-Formats tools from Bioconda bring their own Java, so there is nothing else to install.

  1. Install pixi, following the instructions on https://pixi.sh. On macOS and Linux this is a single command in the terminal:

    curl -fsSL https://pixi.sh/install.sh | sh

    On Windows, run in PowerShell:

    powershell -ExecutionPolicy ByPass -c "irm -useb https://pixi.sh/install.ps1 | iex"

  2. Open a new terminal and install the Bio-Formats tools:

    pixi global install --channel conda-forge --channel bioconda bftools

bfconvert and showinf are now available in every terminal. If you already use conda or micromamba, the same package works there:

micromamba create -n bftools -c conda-forge -c bioconda bftools
micromamba run -n bftools bfconvert ...

Option 2: Bio-Formats with your own Java

  1. Java: Bio-Formats needs Java 11 or newer. If java -version doesn’t work in a terminal, install it, e.g. from https://adoptium.net.
  2. Bio-Formats command line tools: download bftools.zip from the Bio-Formats downloads and unzip it, e.g. to your home folder. The folder contains bfconvert and showinf (on Windows bfconvert.bat and showinf.bat). Add it to your PATH, or call the tools with their full path.

This route gives you the newest Bio-Formats version; the packages of option 1 can lag behind a little.

Option 3: containers (Docker, Podman, Apptainer)

If you already work with containers, run bfconvert from the BioContainers image, which is built from the same Bioconda package. Pick a version tag from https://quay.io/repository/biocontainers/bftools?tab=tags (the images have no latest tag) and mount the folder with your files:

docker run --rm -v "$PWD":/data -w /data quay.io/biocontainers/bftools:<tag> \
  bfconvert -noflat -bigtiff -compression LZW -no-upgrade input.czi output.ome.tif

On computing clusters, where Docker is usually not available, Apptainer (formerly Singularity) runs the same image:

apptainer exec docker://quay.io/biocontainers/bftools:<tag> \
  bfconvert -noflat -bigtiff -compression LZW -no-upgrade input.czi output.ome.tif

Containers are a good fit for pipelines and clusters. Just for converting files on a laptop, Docker is a much bigger installation than options 1 and 2. The images are built for Intel processors; on Apple silicon Macs they run in emulation and are slower.

Images on an OMERO server

If your facility keeps images on an OMERO server, you may not need to convert anything yourself: OMERO can export images as OME-TIFF. Ask your facility how this is set up.

The recommended command 

bfconvert -noflat -bigtiff -compression LZW -no-upgrade input.czi output.ome.tif
  • -noflat keeps resolution pyramids of slide scans together instead of writing them as extra images.
  • -bigtiff allows files larger than 4 GB, and does no harm otherwise.
  • -compression LZW is lossless. Avoid lossy compression for figures.
  • -no-upgrade skips the online check for updates.

Two settings help with some files and computers. Set them once in the terminal before converting:

# an English number format: some locales (e.g. German) make Bio-Formats fail
export JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS="-Duser.language=en -Duser.country=US"
# more memory for large tile or slide scans
export BF_MAX_MEM=4g

On Windows (PowerShell), use $env:JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS = "..." and $env:BF_MAX_MEM = "4g" instead.

Files with several scenes

CZI and LIF files can hold several scenes (positions, wells). Convert each scene into a file of its own with -series (counted from 0):

showinf -nopix -noflat -no-upgrade input.czi | grep "Series count"
#> Series count = 3

bfconvert -noflat -bigtiff -compression LZW -no-upgrade -series 0 input.czi input_s1.ome.tif
bfconvert -noflat -bigtiff -compression LZW -no-upgrade -series 1 input.czi input_s2.ome.tif
bfconvert -noflat -bigtiff -compression LZW -no-upgrade -series 2 input.czi input_s3.ome.tif

Don’t convert all scenes at once with a file name pattern: that writes a multi-file OME-TIFF, whose files refer to each other, and read_images() reads single-file OME-TIFFs only.

A whole folder

This script converts all CZI files of a folder raw_data into a folder ome-tiff, one file per scene (macOS and Linux):

export JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS="-Duser.language=en -Duser.country=US"
export BF_MAX_MEM=4g
mkdir -p ome-tiff

for f in raw_data/*.czi; do
  name=$(basename "$f" .czi)
  n=$(showinf -nopix -noflat -no-upgrade "$f" | sed -n 's/^Series count = //p')
  if [ "$n" = "1" ]; then
    bfconvert -noflat -bigtiff -compression LZW -no-upgrade "$f" "ome-tiff/$name.ome.tif"
  else
    for i in $(seq 0 $((n - 1))); do
      bfconvert -noflat -bigtiff -compression LZW -no-upgrade -series "$i" "$f" "ome-tiff/${name}_s$((i + 1)).ome.tif"
    done
  fi
done

On Windows (PowerShell), for files with one scene each:

$env:JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS = "-Duser.language=en -Duser.country=US"
$env:BF_MAX_MEM = "4g"
New-Item -ItemType Directory -Force ome-tiff | Out-Null

Get-ChildItem raw_data -Filter *.czi | ForEach-Object {
  bfconvert.bat -noflat -bigtiff -compression LZW -no-upgrade $_.FullName "ome-tiff\$($_.BaseName).ome.tif"
}

From R

To keep the conversion in the same script as the figure, call bfconvert from R. Files that were converted before are skipped:

bfconvert <- "bfconvert" # or the full path, e.g. "~/bftools/bfconvert"
Sys.setenv(JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS = "-Duser.language=en -Duser.country=US", BF_MAX_MEM = "4g")

files <- list.files("raw_data", pattern = "\\.czi$", full.names = TRUE)
dir.create("ome-tiff", showWarnings = FALSE)

for (f in files) {
  out <- file.path("ome-tiff", sub("\\.czi$", ".ome.tif", basename(f)))
  if (file.exists(out)) next
  system2(bfconvert, c("-noflat", "-bigtiff", "-compression", "LZW", "-no-upgrade", shQuote(f), shQuote(out)))
}

Check the result

Read the converted files and check where their metadata came from. OME-TIFFs should show ome-xml for both the metadata and the pixel size:

library(tidymontage)
library(dplyr)

read_images("ome-tiff") |>
  distinct(file = basename(filepath), channel, color, pixel_size, meta_source, pixel_size_source)

If meta_source says imagej or tiff, the file was not written as OME-TIFF; most often its name doesn’t end in .ome.tif. If pixel_size is NA, scale bars can’t be drawn: check the calibration in the original file.
